title: The Home That Fits Both of You
subtitle: A shared space works better when it’s designed around the people who actually use it—not an imagined average body.
imageAlt: Two women partners with distinct builds compare notes beside a kitchen counter, with everyday items arranged within easy reach.
imageConcept: Two women partners with distinct builds walk through their home together, noticing a kitchen shelf, a hallway rug and a bathroom light as they discuss small changes that could make shared routines easier.
body: A home is a sequence of small physical negotiations

You reach for a mug, step around a bag, turn into the bathroom, or lean over a counter. Most of the time, these movements barely register. But when a shelf is awkwardly high for one person, a hallway is dim, or a frequently used item is tucked behind something else, the space quietly asks one person to do more work than the other.

That friction doesn’t mean either partner is doing anything wrong. Bodies differ in height, reach, strength, balance, mobility and comfort, and those differences can change over time. A useful shared home doesn’t demand that both people move in exactly the same way. It makes ordinary tasks workable for the people who live there.

AARP’s HomeFit guide is intended to help make homes comfortable and safe for older adults and people of all ages, a useful reminder that usability is not reserved for one life stage [1]. The goal here is not to turn your home into a project or diagnose a problem. It’s to notice where a small adjustment could make a routine easier for both of you.
Walk the routines, not the floor plan

Choose one everyday route at a time: coming in with groceries, making breakfast, getting ready for bed, or moving from the bedroom to the bathroom at night. Each partner can walk the route as they normally would, without trying to correct or coach the other person. Pay attention to what the routine actually requires: reaching, gripping, bending, stepping over, carrying, turning, or seeing in low light.

Keep the observation specific. “The hallway is annoying” is harder to act on than “I can’t see the edge of the rug when I come in after dark.” “The kitchen doesn’t work” is less useful than “The bowls I use every morning are on the highest shelf.” AARP’s HomeFit download page also links to worksheets [1].

Then trade routes. The point is not to prove that one person has the harder home or to produce a single verdict. You’re gathering two accounts of the same environment. One partner may find a counter comfortable while the other has to lean; one may move confidently through a room that feels cluttered to the other.
Make a friction list before making changes

Write down what happened, where it happened and what would make it easier. Separate observations from assumptions. “I nearly caught my foot on this loose rug” describes an event. “You’re clumsy” assigns blame and tells you nothing about the room. Try noting how often the issue comes up and whether it affects one person, both, or a guest who may use the space differently.

For each item, ask: Is this a reach problem, a grip problem, a visibility problem, a tight turn, an unstable surface, or simply an inconvenient location? A low-cost fix often becomes clearer when you name the task. Moving daily dishes to a lower shelf may help more than reorganizing every cupboard. Shifting a chair may open a turning path without changing the room.

This is also a good moment to ask whether a proposed fix would create new friction for someone else. Moving an object within one person’s reach could put it in another’s way. A shared home is not a test of whose preference wins; it’s a place to look for arrangements that meet the most important needs without adding unnecessary obstacles.
Start with the parts of the home you use most

The kitchen is a useful place to begin because routines repeat there. Put the dishes, cups, cooking tools and ingredients used most often where the people who use them can reach without stretching, climbing or moving several other things. If two people have different preferred setups, consider giving each a clearly defined area rather than forcing every item into one universal arrangement. Keep heavy or frequently handled objects easy to access, and leave a clear place to set down a hot pan or a grocery bag.

At the entry, look at shoes, bags, packages and the route from the door. A landing spot for keys or a bag can prevent objects from migrating into a walkway. In shared living areas, notice whether charging cords cross a route or whether furniture makes a usual turn tight. These are small design questions with a direct relationship to daily ease.

Lighting and rugs deserve a deliberate look. The National Institute on Aging lists better lighting, removing area rugs, and fixing carpets firmly to the floor among home-safety changes for older adults [2]. That guidance is specifically framed around older adults, but the observations—whether a surface shifts or a route is hard to see—can prompt a useful conversation in any household. They are starting points, not a universal assessment or a guarantee against falls.
Give bathrooms and nighttime routes their own attention

Bathrooms combine wet surfaces, close quarters and movements that can involve turning, bending or stepping over an edge. Check whether the floor gets slick, whether towels and toiletries are reachable, whether the light switch is easy to find, and whether the doorway or space around the sink feels cramped to either person. A bath mat that slides is a different issue from a shower that is difficult to enter; naming the specific task helps you choose an appropriate response.

For nighttime routes, walk from bed to bathroom with the lighting conditions you usually have. Notice dark corners, cords, laundry baskets, pets’ water bowls or other objects that appear in the path. Improving the light or moving an obstruction may be a straightforward first step. The National Institute on Aging’s home-safety guidance for older adults recommends measures such as better lighting, removing area rugs or securing carpets, and installing grab bars near toilets and in tubs or showers [2]. Those recommendations address older-adult fall prevention; they shouldn’t be treated as a universal safety checklist or as proof that every household needs the same equipment.

If a change involves installation, the right solution depends on the person, the room and the product. Don’t assume that a decorative handle or a loose accessory will provide support. For a modification intended to bear weight, seek qualified guidance about what is appropriate and how it should be installed.
Try reversible changes before taking on a renovation

Once you have a short list, choose one adjustment that is easy to test and undo. Move a frequently used item to a more comfortable shelf. Improve a dark corner with an appropriate lamp. Secure or remove a rug that shifts. Reposition a hamper or small table that narrows a route. Then use the space normally for several days and ask each other what changed: Did the task take fewer awkward movements? Did the new arrangement make another routine harder? Is the improvement useful enough to keep?

Testing one change at a time makes the result easier to understand. It also keeps the conversation practical: you’re evaluating an arrangement, not deciding who was right. If a move doesn’t help, put things back and try a different option. A home can be adjusted in stages, and a workable solution may be simpler than a full redesign.

For larger changes—such as widening a doorway, adding a ramp or changing a fixture—pause before buying materials or starting work. Check lease terms, local requirements and any relevant building rules. If installation or construction is involved, consult a qualified professional. The right plan depends on the home and the intended use; this walkthrough is not a substitute for technical advice.
When the need is bigger than a quick fix

Some needs call for professional input, especially when a person’s mobility or circumstances have changed, when a modification must support someone’s weight, or when the home’s layout is the main obstacle. Describe the task that is difficult and the conditions around it before asking for help: where it happens, what movement is involved, and what the person wants to be able to do. That gives a provider a clearer starting point than a broad request to make the home accessible.

The Administration for Community Living says its Home Modification Information Network is a free resource for finding programs, funding opportunities, service providers and other resources at local, state and national levels, with searches by need and ZIP code [3]. Availability and suitability will vary, so treat a listing as a place to investigate rather than a promise of eligibility or a recommendation for a particular contractor. If you rent, include the landlord or property manager early and check applicable requirements before making changes.
End with one route you can both live with

Choose a single routine you both care about—bringing groceries in, making coffee, or getting from bed to the bathroom—and walk it together once more. Each person names one moment that feels easy and one moment that could work better. Agree on one reversible change, decide who will make it, and set a day to check whether it helped. If you disagree, keep the change small enough to test rather than turning the discussion into a permanent verdict. The useful outcome is not a perfectly optimized home. It is a space shaped by what its occupants notice, value and can actually use.
